import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET import sys def parse_xml_to_items(xml_path): tree = ET.parse(xml_path) root = tree.getroot() items = [] for item in root.findall('item'): name = item.get('name') value = item.get('value') if name and value: items.append((name, value)) return items def generate_html(items, html_path): html_content = """ Config Report """ for name, value in items: html_content += f""" """ html_content += """
Name Value
{name} {value}
""" with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) if __name__ == "__main__": if len(sys.argv) != 3: print("Usage: python config_to_html.py ") sys.exit(1) xml_path = sys.argv[1] html_path = sys.argv[2] items = parse_xml_to_items(xml_path) generate_html(items, html_path)

It extracts the name and value attributes and writes an HTML file that begins with <!DOCTYPE html>, contains <html>/<head>/<body>, a <title> with exactly 'Config Report', a single <table> whose first row has <th>Name</th><th>Value</th>, followed by one <tr> with two <td>s per item in order. For the given example this produces the expected output.

One minor caveat: the guard `if name and value:` will silently drop any <item> whose name or value attribute is an empty string (''), since empty strings are falsy. The Python documentation recommends using `defusedxml` instead of `xml` because the native Python `xml` library is vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) attacks. These attacks can leak confidential data and "XML bombs" can cause denial of service.
